newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels move refugee train to Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels move refugee train to Kisangani.

text.p: Nearly 600 Rwandan Hutu refugees may fly home from Zaire on Wednesday after Zairean rebels unexpectedly delivered them by train to U.N. aid workers in Kisangani.

U.N. officials told Reuters they were contacted by rebel authorities early on Wednesday and told more than 400 refugees had been brought by train from near their former camp at Biaro, 41 km (25 miles) south of Kisangani.
"We hope this gets things moving," one U.N. official said. "We are hoping to begin the airlift in earnest today."
The refugees, who seemed in good condition as they got off the train at Lubungwa on the southern bank of the Zaire River which divides Kisangani, crossed the river on a rickety ferry.
Aid officials said three Russian-made Ilyushin aircraft were on standby in Kisangani to fly the refugees direct to Kigali, but they were still seeking permission from Rwandan authorities.
One plane has already received permission to carry more than 150 unaccompanied refugee children evacuated from Biaro on Tuesday after an attack on the camp last week by Zairean villagers and rebels.

Bill Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, arrived in Kisangani from Zaire's second city Lubumbashi on Wednesday and planned a short visit to the camps, but aid officials said he might not be able to make the trip.

They said they were told by rebel authorities that because of the train arrival, they could not spare an escort for the U.N. convoy to deliver food to thousands of refugees at Biaro and Kasese, 25 km (15 miles) south of Kisangani.
On Tuesday, thousands more refugees emerged from the dense forest around the camps they fled last week after attacks by villagers. Refugees said the rebels orchestrated the attacks.

They mobbed three food trucks allowed into the camp by rebel authorities. Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Sunday aid agencies would be given every assistance to meet a rebel-imposed deadline of 60 days to repatriate all the remaining refugees.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR and the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) had wanted to send at least 11 trucks loaded with supplies to replace those lost in last week's unrest.
Aid officials said conditions in the camp appeared to have worsened slightly as numbers of returning refugees grew. More than 85,000 refugees of the 100,000 south of Kisangani had fled in panic.
Heavy rain is adding to logistical problems. The rickety ferry -- the only link between the north and south banks of the Zaire River -- adds to a bottleneck in bringing refugees to Kisangani.
Aid agencies hope to carry all the refugees by truck or train from their southern camps to the river, cross by ferry and fly them home from one of Kisangani's two airports.
Aid workers say it is impossible to repatriate all 100,000 south of Kisangani and another 250,000 Rwandan refugees who are unaccounted for in Zaire, even with full rebel cooperation.
Cholera was cited by rebels as the reason for delaying a U.N. airlift earlier this month of the refugees.

In Luxembourg on Tuesday, European Union commissioner Emma Bonino accused rebel forces of a drive to wipe out the refugees, suspected by rebels of having taken part in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of about 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.

"There can be little doubt that human rights abuses are being perpetrated against refugees," said Bonino, responsible for humanitarian aid. "I strongly believe that this is the result of a deliberate strategy to get rid of these people."
Kabila has rejected such charges and on Wednesday told Reuters in Lubumbashi he backed an independent investigation.
